problem: Existing embodied benchmarks test exploration, interaction, and spatial memory in isolation (VLN instruction following, tabletop manipulation, outdoor goal reaching with known destinations), so it is unclear how failures compound when these capabilities must be composed in a realistic search-and-rescue workflow.
motivation: Real SAR needs autonomous exploration under ambiguous multimodal clues, multi-stage interaction, and return-by-memory over large indoor/outdoor and multi-floor spaces. A sequentially dependent benchmark with stage-level scoring can reveal where and why agents fail, and an automatic pipeline can supply training data with interaction annotations.
key_idea: RescueBench composes SAR into four sequentially dependent stages (explore, locate-and-rescue, memory-guided return, locate-and-handoff) across five difficulty levels in photo-realistic UE5 scenes, with stage-level scoring and an automatic episode generation and annotation pipeline.
insight: Stage-level decomposition shows S1 (exploration) is the dominant bottleneck, since S2 and S4 track S1 within 0-3 points. S3 (return by memory) is a second, independent bottleneck: ROCKET-2 (ft) drops from 17.6 (S2) to 8.8 (S3) at L3. Fine-tuning on about 400K automatically collected steps helps mainly at L1 and gains vanish at L4/L5, which the authors read as an architectural limit, not a data limit; this is an interpretation not isolated by controlled ablation.
method: Four-stage task: S1 explore from sparse multimodal clues (visual snapshot + text) with no coordinates; S2 reach and rescue the target; S3 return to the ambulance from memory; S4 locate the ambulance and hand off. Full success requires all four stages.

Environment-assisted interaction triggering: within 1.5 m the pick/drop interaction fires automatically for all methods except ROCKET-2, which uses native actions, isolating navigation from manipulation.

Five difficulty levels: L1-L2 close-range targets in clean vs cluttered scenes; L3 mid-range occluded targets needing search; L4 cross-region with doors; L5 multi-floor. Distance ranges and validation filters (elevation change, interaction elements) per level; clue ambiguity grows from visual matching to directional to hierarchical.

Metrics: TCR (all four stages succeed), Task Score 0-100 (25 per stage, proportional to distance progress), average time and steps, collision count, and Human Similarity (DTW-based trajectory similarity to human demonstrations).

Automatic data pipeline: sample spawn zones from the UE5 navmesh, sample ambulance/target/agent under level constraints, a navmesh agent with a state machine runs the four stages recording RGB/depth/segmentation, waypoints and interaction annotations, then validates difficulty; Qwen-3.5 Plus writes clues from egocentric video.

Baselines and references: LLM-YOLO Planner, Uni-NaVid, ViNT, NoMaD, SG-Nav, OmniNav, ROCKET-2 (four of them fine-tuned), plus human players and an Oracle Navigator; the test set has 213 episodes over 7 UnrealZoo scenes.

setting.backbone: Benchmark paper; evaluated baselines include GPT-4o+YOLO planner (zero-shot), Uni-NaVid, ViNT, NoMaD, ROCKET-2 (fine-tuned and zero-shot), SG-Nav and OmniNav (zero-shot)
setting.training_data: Baselines fine-tuned on about 400K automatically collected expert steps (9:1 train/val split); others zero-shot with original pretrained weights
setting.observation: synchronized egocentric RGB + depth + semantic segmentation, plus sparse multimodal clue (image + text)
setting.action_space: continuous forward and angular velocity plus 3 binary interaction actions (pick, drop, open door)
setting.simulator: Unreal Engine 5.6 with UnrealCV / UnrealZoo (7 scenes)
setting.privileged: none for the baselines; the Oracle reference uses ground-truth target and ambulance locations and shortest path

numbers_note: The paper is a new benchmark (RescueBench, 213 test episodes) that does not map onto any canonical benchmark name in the list; its metrics are TCR/TS and it has no SR/SPL. Per-method results are baselines, not the paper's own method, so nothing is recorded.
results: No baseline completes the full task at L5 (TCR 0.0 for every baseline; the human player reaches 93.5). ROCKET-2 (fine-tuned) gets the highest L3 TS (52.0, TCR 15.0), and Uni-NaVid fine-tuning raises L1 TCR from 24.0 to 52.0. ViNT and NoMaD go from 0 to 8.0 at L1, and every learned baseline is near zero TS at L4-L5.
limitations: Small test set (213 episodes, 7 scenes); environment-assisted interaction triggering abstracts away manipulation, and only single-agent evaluation is primary (multi-agent is preliminary).

The claim that limitations are architectural rather than data-driven rests on a single fine-tuning setup (about 400K steps), with no controlled ablation, and baselines are used with their default inputs and different latencies under a wall-clock time budget, which confounds slow map-based methods.
No real-robot validation, and the conclusions are for the evaluated method families only.
